source_refs.note: Book p. 88: Unit 6 INTRODUCTION (aims, number patterns (i)-(iv), explanation) and 6.1 Sequence (definition, terms, general term). Teaching notes, About this unit, Key points, Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: In this unit we learn to analyse and solve problems on arithmetic, geometric and harmonic sequences and series, including their real-world uses. We shall identify different types of sequences, find finite and infinite sums, and use sigma notation. The unit also looks at practical situations such as motor vehicle leasing, investment planning and other financial calculations, and at uses in fields like healthcare, finance and traffic modelling. By the end, you should be able to solve both theoretical and real-life problems with sequences and series.
Let us observe the following patterns of numbers.

In pattern (i), every number (except the first number 5) is formed by adding 6 to the previous number. So a definite pattern is followed in the arrangement of these numbers. Similarly, in pattern (ii) every number is obtained by multiplying the previous number by 2. Patterns (iii) and (iv) also follow fixed rules. When a set of numbers follows a pattern and there is a clear rule for finding the next number, we have a sequence, as in the examples above.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Find the rule of each pattern by comparing a term with the one before it:
(i) add 6: \(5 + 6 = 11\), \(11 + 6 = 17\). Next term \(23 + 6 = 29\).
(ii) multiply by 2: \(6 \times 2 = 12\). Next term \(48 \times 2 = 96\).
(iii) subtract 2 (that is, add \(-2\)): next term \(-4 - 2 = -6\).
(iv) multiply by \(\frac{2}{3}\): \(\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{4}{9}\). Next term \(\frac{16}{81} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{32}{243}\).
Patterns (i) and (iii) grow by adding a fixed number; (ii) and (iv) grow by multiplying by a fixed number. These two kinds are the arithmetic and geometric progressions of this unit.

A systematic arrangement of numbers according to a given rule is called a sequence. The numbers in a sequence are called its terms. We call the first term of a sequence \(a_{1}\), the second term \(a_{2}\), and so on. The \(n\)th term of a sequence is denoted by \(a_{n}\); it is also called the general term of the sequence. The terms just before it are called the \((n-1)\)st term, the \((n-2)\)nd term, and so on.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read \(a_{n}\) as "a sub n". The small number \(n\) is only the position of the term (1st, 2nd, 3rd, ...), it is not a power and not a multiplier. So \(a_{3}\) means "the third term", not \(a \times 3\).
The general term is a rule that gives any term from its position. For pattern (i): \(a_{n} = 6n - 1\). Check: \(a_{1} = 6 - 1 = 5\), \(a_{2} = 12 - 1 = 11\), \(a_{3} = 17\), \(a_{4} = 23\).
Because \(n\) takes the values \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\), a sequence is really a rule (a function) whose inputs are the natural numbers. The whole sequence is often written \(\{a_{n}\}\).
If \(n\) is the position of a term, the term just before it is in position \(n - 1\) and the one before that in position \(n - 2\): \(a_{n-1}\), \(a_{n-2}\).

blocks.title: About this unit
blocks.text:
Route through Unit 6: 6.1 sequences, 6.2 and 6.3 arithmetic progression and arithmetic means, 6.4 series (sums), 6.5 to 6.7 geometric progression, geometric means and geometric series, then arithmetico-geometric and harmonic progressions and their uses.
Skills you need from earlier classes: substituting numbers into an expression, solving linear equations, and simplifying fractions and surds.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A sequence is an arrangement of numbers that follows a definite rule.
2. Its numbers are called terms: \(a_{1}\) is the first term, \(a_{2}\) the second, \(a_{n}\) the \(n\)th or general term.
3. The terms before \(a_{n}\) are \(a_{n-1}\) (the \((n-1)\)st term), \(a_{n-2}\) (the \((n-2)\)nd term), and so on.
4. To find the rule of a pattern, compare each term with the term before it (difference or ratio).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Reading \(a_{n}\) as \(a \times n\) or \(a^{n}\): the subscript is only the position of the term.
2. Thinking any list of numbers is a sequence: there must be a clear rule for the next term.
3. Writing \(a_{n} - 1\) when the previous term \(a_{n-1}\) is meant: \(a_{n} - 1\) is "the \(n\)th term minus one", a different thing.
